::: {.kw-overview}
This issue focuses predominantly on strategies to reduce ischaemic injury in deceased-donor kidneys. Two cohort studies evaluated normothermic techniques in donation after circulatory death (DCD). In donors aged 50 years or older, abdominal normothermic regional perfusion and ex situ normothermic machine perfusion were associated with comparable rates of delayed graft function, affecting approximately half of recipients. A single-region US series reported lower odds of delayed graft function with normothermic regional perfusion than with super-rapid recovery, despite an older donor population. A paired-donor study from India examined the retrieval sequence itself: removing one kidney before aortic cross-clamping reduced cold ischaemia time from approximately five hours to just over one hour. On donor utilisation, a meta-analysis of 457 recipients found that the risk of transmitting a multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organism was determined by the anatomical relationship between the site of colonisation and the graft, rather than by the resistance profile. In perioperative care, a randomised trial showed that Ringer's lactate preserved serum bicarbonate more effectively than a chloride-reduced saline–dextrose regimen and was associated with a higher eGFR at one month. The remaining studies address access to transplantation and rejection. A registry analysis of more than 180,000 transplants demonstrated a graded association between recipient obesity and delayed graft function; New Zealand data showed that candidates with a cPRA of 99% or above were transplanted at one-tenth the rate of those below 80%; and a Medicare claims study of almost 93,000 recipients ranked rejection phenotypes by their impact on graft survival.
:::

### 1. [Abdominal Normothermic Regional Perfusion Versus Normothermic Machine Perfusion of DCD Kidneys Aged 50 Years or Older: A Propensity Score Matched Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1111/aor.70234)
[Slagter JS, van de Geijn EF, de Goeij FHC, Groen PC, Schurink IJ, Alwyn IPJ, Porte RJ, Huurman VAL, de Jonge J, Minnee RC. *Artif Organs*, 2026. PMID: 42864868.]{.kw-ref}

Kidneys from older circulatory-death donors are used less often because they are more vulnerable to ischaemia–reperfusion injury, and the authors note that oxygenated hypothermic machine perfusion helps only partly. This study compared the two normothermic options now competing for that role. Kidneys from donors aged 50 or over that underwent abdominal normothermic regional perfusion in the donor (85 kidneys, from a national registry) were compared with kidneys that underwent ex situ normothermic machine perfusion (29 kidneys, from two clinical trials), using propensity score matching. Delayed graft function, the primary outcome, was common and similar in both groups: 46% after regional perfusion and 52% after machine perfusion (p = 0.82). Primary non-function (8% against 7%) and acute rejection (25% against 31%) did not differ either, and death-censored graft survival and patient survival were comparable. At three years, median eGFR was 38 mL/min/1.73 m² in the regional perfusion group and 33 mL/min/1.73 m² in the machine perfusion group. The authors note that the study is not randomised and is small, and the two arms come from different data sources, so the result shows that both techniques are feasible rather than that they are equivalent. For UK centres weighing normothermic strategies for older DCD kidneys, the study gives no clear reason to prefer one technique over the other, so the choice may come down to logistics and local availability.

### 2. [Early Transplant Outcomes and Kidney Donor Profile Index Risk Prediction Performance in Kidneys Recovered Using a Uniform Abdominal Normothermic Regional Perfusion Technique](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70729)
[Selim MA, Buff M, Fenlon M, Forbes A, Nwaduru C, Ovalle LA, Kohler R, Horns JJ, Botha J, Zimmerman MA. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42912555.]{.kw-ref}

The kidney donor profile index gives every circulatory-death kidney the same risk weighting, so it cannot account for differences in how the kidney was recovered. This retrospective study from a single US donation service area looked at all kidney transplants from donors procured between January 2023 and December 2024. There were 523 transplants: 310 from brain-dead donors, 122 from circulatory-death donors recovered by super-rapid recovery, and 91 from circulatory-death donors recovered with a single standardised abdominal regional perfusion technique. The regional perfusion donors were older (median age 55, against 43.5 for super-rapid recovery and 38 for brain-dead donors) and had higher donor profile index scores (66%, 53% and 27%). In multivariable models restricted to circulatory-death donors, regional perfusion was associated with lower odds of delayed graft function than super-rapid recovery (odds ratio 0.445, 95% confidence interval 0.23 to 0.861). Each point of donor profile index raised the odds of delayed function (odds ratio 1.028 per point). One-year overall graft survival did not differ by recovery method. Interaction modelling suggested that regional perfusion kidneys had lower delayed function odds than super-rapid recovery kidneys at the same index value, but the interaction term was not statistically significant, so the study cannot show that the index performs differently after regional perfusion. Follow-up was only one year. For UK practice, where risk scoring of DCD offers similarly does not account for recovery technique, the study suggests that a kidney recovered with regional perfusion may carry less early risk than its donor score implies, which is a reason to collect technique-specific outcome data nationally.

### 3. [Sequential Kidney-First Retrieval and Early Graft Outcomes in Deceased Donor Kidney Transplantation: A Paired-Donor Comparative Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.6002/ect.2026.0219)
[Kolte S, Kashiv P, Kriplani A, Munjewar C, Bhawane A, Khetan P, Khandekar AK, Deshpande N, Pasari A, Balwani M. *Exp Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42885705.]{.kw-ref}

In standard multiorgan retrieval the kidneys come out last, which adds to their cold ischaemia time. This retrospective study from collaborating centres in central India tested a different sequence in 44 brain-dead donors transplanted between January 2018 and December 2024. One kidney from each donor was removed from the heart-beating donor before aortic cross-clamping. The other was removed in the usual way, after the thoracic and other abdominal organs. Because each donor provided one kidney to each arm, the 88 recipients form a paired comparison that controls for donor quality. Cold ischaemia was much shorter with kidney-first retrieval: mean 78 minutes, against 299 minutes. First-hour urine output was about twice as high (374 against 186 mL), mean day-8 creatinine was 1.3 against 3.1 mg/dL, and delayed graft function needing dialysis fell from 36.4% to 9.1% (p = 0.002). Retrieval injuries and post-transplant complications together fell from 38.6% to 6.8%. Benefits of similar size were seen with kidneys from expanded-criteria donors. In multivariable analysis, removing the kidney last independently predicted delayed graft function (adjusted odds ratio 3.92, 95% confidence interval 1.41 to 10.87). The authors report that other organs were procured without compromise, but the abstract gives no thoracic or liver outcome data, the study is retrospective, and the cold ischaemia times in both arms are short by most standards, which may limit how far the results transfer to other systems. For UK multiorgan retrieval teams, the paper is mainly a prompt to look again at retrieval sequence and the warm-to-cold transition, but a technique that changes how thoracic and liver teams work would need prospective evidence, including outcomes for the other organs, before anyone adopted it.

### 4. [Risk of Donor-Derived Infections From Organ Donors Colonized or Infected With Multidrug-Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70714)
[Paraskevas T, Chatzigrigoriadis C, Kostakis ID, Karydis N, Papasotiriou M, Ntrinias T, Maroulis I, Marangos M, Papachristou E, Grossi PA, Assimakopoulos SF. *Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42873093.]{.kw-ref}

Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organisms are being found more often in potential donors, and national guidance on whether to use these organs differs, with Spanish and Scandinavian guidelines more restrictive than the American and European society positions. This review searched PubMed and Scopus for observational studies published from 2010 to 2025 and found 12 cohort studies covering 457 solid organ recipients, 178 of them kidney recipients. All the studies were of deceased donors, and several were Chinese kidney series of carbapenem-resistant *Klebsiella* found in preservation fluid. Across all studies, 29% of exposed recipients developed a donor-derived infection (95% confidence interval 11% to 49%; I² = 91.7%). When recipients were classed by exposure, the picture was clear. In high-risk scenarios (donor bacteraemia, a positive preservation fluid culture, or a positive culture from the organ itself) the transmission rate was 40%. When the organism was found only at a site unrelated to the graft, the rate was effectively zero (0%, 95% confidence interval 0% to 1%, across 128 recipients). A positive preservation fluid culture carried the highest risk, at 58%, against 19% for donor bacteraemia. The pooled estimate for kidney transplants was 23%. Ninety-day mortality was 49% in recipients with a confirmed donor-derived infection and 6% in exposed recipients without one. The review is limited by aggregate data, small single-centre studies and inconsistent reporting of antimicrobial treatment. For UK kidney teams, the practical message is that a donor carrying a resistant organism at a site unrelated to the kidney should not on its own be a reason to decline, whereas a positive preservation fluid or urine culture needs prompt communication between centres and targeted treatment of the recipient.

### 5. [Randomized Clinical Trial of Ringer's Lactate Versus Chloride-Reduced Saline-Dextrose in Postoperative Kidney Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2026.107081)
[Sawasdichai K, Rakpithayanon C, Konwai S, Wuttiputhanun T, Lumlertgul N, Apisutimaitri K, Burimsittichai R, Vorasittha A, Pobpan P, Tasanarong A, Leelahavanichkul A, Townamchai N, Praditpornsilpa K, Eiam-Ong S, Avihingsanon Y, Udomkarnjananun S. *Kidney Int Rep*, 2026. PMID: 42898223.]{.kw-ref}

Many fluid trials in transplantation have compared a balanced crystalloid with plain saline, a comparison that tends to favour the balanced fluid. This open-label trial at a Bangkok centre used a stronger comparator. Adult first-transplant recipients were randomised, stratified by donor type, to postoperative Ringer's lactate or to a dual infusion of normal saline and 5% dextrose designed to limit chloride load. Both fluids were titrated 1:1 to hourly urine output. From September 2024 to March 2026, 159 patients were randomised, and the prespecified modified intention-to-treat analysis included the 134 who received at least 2 litres of study fluid (67 per arm, 68.7% deceased-donor). Total fluid volumes were similar, at about 9.5 to 9.9 litres. On day 4, mean serum bicarbonate was 19.39 mEq/L with Ringer's lactate against 17.31 mEq/L with saline–dextrose (p < 0.001), and venous pH was 7.41 against 7.37. Rescue bicarbonate was needed by 17.9% against 58.2% of patients. Mean eGFR at one month was 61.63 against 53.18 mL/min/1.73 m² (p = 0.028). Delayed graft function was 3.0% against 9.0%, which was not significant, and the full text indicates that most of the functional and biomarker differences were in deceased-donor recipients. Hyperkalaemia and hyperglycaemia were uncommon in both arms. The trial is single-centre and open-label. It also excluded the 25 recipients who were oligo-anuric from the start, so it has little to say about the recipients most likely to develop delayed graft function, and serum lactate was not routinely measured. For UK units, the trial supports a single balanced crystalloid after transplantation, with Ringer's lactate as an inexpensive option, and the low, similar rates of hyperkalaemia in both arms are relevant to units that still avoid potassium-containing fluids.

### 6. [Beyond Body Mass Index Cutoffs: Donor Quality and Ischemic Burden Shape Kidney Transplant Outcomes in Recipients With Severe Obesity: An Analysis of the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients Dataset](https://doi.org/10.6002/ect.2026.0093)
[Sharma R, Dwivedi AK. *Exp Clin Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42885701.]{.kw-ref}

Body mass index thresholds are still used to limit access to transplant listing, although the evidence behind specific cut-offs is thin. This analysis used aggregate Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients summary tables for US deceased-donor kidney transplants performed from 2014 to 2024. Recipients were grouped by body mass index as below 35, 35 to 40, and above 40. Among 180,849 transplants (131,379 from brain-dead donors and 49,470 from circulatory-death donors), delayed graft function rose with each group: 29.3%, 37.8% and 42.4% (p < 0.001). Compared with a body mass index below 35, the odds ratio for delayed function was 1.46 (95% confidence interval 1.42 to 1.51) for 35 to 40 and 1.77 (1.65 to 1.90) for above 40. For brain-dead donor kidneys, five-year graft survival fell from 77.51% to 74.33% to 70.03% across the three groups. The disadvantage of higher body mass index was present at every level of donor profile index, donor age and cold ischaemia time, and the authors judge it largest when obesity was combined with poorer donor or ischaemic factors. The analysis relies on aggregate tables with Kaplan–Meier estimates and unadjusted comparisons, not on patient-level multivariable models, so other recipient factors that travel with obesity are not accounted for. It also does not compare transplanted obese patients with similar patients who stayed on dialysis, which is the comparison that decides whether listing is worthwhile. For UK units weighing listing decisions, the paper argues for matching severely obese recipients with lower-risk kidneys and short cold ischaemia rather than excluding them on body mass index alone.

### 7. [Rates of Deceased Donor Kidney Transplantation in Highly Sensitised Patients in Aotearoa New Zealand: A Data Linkage Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1111/nep.70295)
[Thomas AOR, Hedley JA, Shettigar R, Cross NB, Dittmer I, Dunckley H, Webster AC. *Nephrology (Carlton)*, 2026. PMID: 42878695.]{.kw-ref}

This study was designed to inform possible changes to New Zealand's national kidney allocation scheme by showing how highly sensitised candidates have fared under it. The authors used linked health data from the AcceSS and Equity in Transplantation platform to identify everyone listed for a deceased-donor kidney between 2006 and 2019. Patients were classed as highly sensitised if their panel reactive antibody or calculated panel reactive antibody was 80% or higher, and this group was split into 80–94%, 95–98% and 99% or above. A previous transplant, female sex, younger age and non-European ethnicity were all associated with higher sensitisation (each p < 0.001). The rate of transplantation fell as sensitisation rose. Compared with candidates below 80%, the hazard ratio for transplantation was 0.75 at 80–94% (95% confidence interval 0.54 to 1.04, not significant), 0.38 at 95–98% (0.23 to 0.60) and 0.10 at 99% or above (0.05 to 0.17). The abstract does not give absolute numbers in each group, waiting times, or how much of the gap living donation or desensitisation filled. Because the study ends in 2019, it also predates any recent changes to allocation. The authors identify the 99%-and-above group as the obvious target for change. For UK clinicians reviewing how allocation treats sensitised patients, the data show that the real disadvantage is concentrated at the very top of the range, which supports targeting allocation priority at candidates with cPRA of 99% or more rather than spreading it across everyone above 80%.

### 8. [Claims-Based Phenotyping of Acute Kidney Transplant Rejection in a National Medicare Cohort](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2026.107060)
[Ekanayake C, Yu M, Natarajan K, Husain SA, Muppavarapu CS, Schold J, Mohan S. *Kidney Int Rep*, 2026. PMID: 42898365.]{.kw-ref}

Transplant registries usually record acute rejection as a simple yes or no, which says nothing about how outcomes differ by rejection type. This study used US Renal Data System claims for 92,845 adult first kidney-only recipients transplanted from 2012 to 2021 with Medicare as primary payer. Rejection in the first year was identified from transplant-complication codes combined with antirejection treatment within 14 days. The type of treatment was used to infer the phenotype: intravenous steroids alone for mild cellular rejection, thymoglobulin for severe cellular rejection, plasmapheresis with or without immunoglobulin for antibody-mediated rejection, and a combination for mixed rejection. Of 5,712 episodes, 69.4% were classed as mild cellular, 8.8% severe cellular, 19.7% antibody-mediated and 2.1% mixed. For the 3,052 episodes preceded by a biopsy, three-year death-censored graft survival was 87.9% for mild cellular, 80.7% for severe cellular, 73.5% for antibody-mediated and 68.4% for mixed rejection. In adjusted time-varying Cox models, the corresponding hazard ratios for graft failure compared with recipients without rejection were 1.84, 2.50, 4.18 and 4.59. Without a preceding biopsy the ranking was less consistent, and severe cellular rejection then carried no excess risk after adjustment, which suggests misclassification when histology is missing. The algorithm was not checked against pathology reports, and the cohort excludes privately insured recipients. For UK practice, the size of the antibody-mediated and mixed rejection penalty supports early biopsy and intensive follow-up after these episodes, and the study shows how much more useful national registry data on rejection would be if they recorded rejection type and treatment.
